intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “The Life of Trust (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of George Müller, who cared for thousands of orphans in England by asking no one but God for what they needed. It works for a small family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and suits ages 6–12.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready; none of the activities use food. The story is full of children without a mother or father, and some children in your group may be fostered, adopted, or living without a parent, so speak warmly and matter-of-factly about the orphans, never ask anyone about their own family, and keep coming back to the book’s own point: God sees every child, cares for every child, and is never late.

weeks.summary: As a boy, George Müller stole from his father and hid a coin in his shoe; as he grew older he told lies, spent money he didn’t have, and at sixteen was even put in prison for a while. The story begins with all these wrong things because it makes what God did next so wonderful. Keep any talk about wrongdoing general, and never ask a child to say aloud what they have done wrong. The big idea: nobody is too bad for God, because God loves to change hearts.

memory_verse.text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned everyone to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

activity.title: A Heart Made New
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half like a card.
On the outside, draw a grey, scribbly cloud to stand for the wrong things we all do. You do not need to write what they are.
Open the card and draw a big, bright heart on the inside.
Write “God loves to change hearts” under the heart, and take the card home.

weeks.summary: As a young man, George went shyly with a friend to a house where Christians met to read the Bible, sing and pray, and for the first time he saw a man kneel to pray. The kind host told him, “Come as often as you please. My house and my heart are open to you,” and George went home peaceful and happy, the turning point of his life. The big idea: God’s heart is open to us, and we never have to be good enough first; we just have to come.

memory_verse.text: He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.

activity.title: The Open Door
steps: Fold both sides of a sheet of paper in towards the middle so they make two doors that open.
Draw handles and decorations on the outside of the doors.
Open the doors and draw a warm, bright room inside with a welcome mat.
Write “Come as often as you please” inside, and remember that God’s door is always open to you.

weeks.summary: George told two old friends about God, but they shrugged and said they didn’t feel they were sinners. Unable to change their minds, he knelt and prayed for them, then kept praying in his bedroom, and when he came back both friends were crying and said they needed God too. The big idea: when we can’t change something ourselves, we can pray, and God can.

memory_verse.text: Jesus, looking at them, said, with men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.

activity.title: My Prayer Bookmark
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half lengthways, and then in half lengthways again, to make a long, thin bookmark.
Write “I can’t, but God can” at the top and decorate the edges.
Underneath, write or draw one or two people you would love to know God. Nobody else needs to see.
Keep the bookmark in a book you read often, and pray for those people each time you see it.

weeks.summary: As a grown-up preacher, George stopped taking wages and made a firm rule: he would never ask anyone for money, only God. When he and his wife were down to a few coins, they knelt and told God, and a few hours later a woman came to the door with money she said God had put in her heart to give two weeks earlier. The big idea: God knows what we need before we ask, so we can tell him about anything and trust him to take care of us.

memory_verse.text: My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Needs and Wants
steps: Explain that a need is something we truly must have, and a want is something nice we would like.
Call out things one at a time, such as a warm coat, a new toy, a bed to sleep in, a bigger bike, friends, a video game. Children stand up for a need and stay sitting for a want.
When a few disagree, stop and talk about it kindly; there is not always one right answer.
Finish by saying the memory verse together: God promises to supply every need.

weeks.summary: One Sunday George and his wife had only a few pennies and barely enough bread for the day, so George asked God very simply for bread for that evening. While he was still praying, a poor woman knocked at the door with some of her own dinner and a little money, and later she came back with a big loaf. The big idea: Jesus taught us to ask for our daily bread, and God cares about ordinary, everyday needs.

memory_verse.text: Give us this day our daily bread.

activity.title: God in My Everyday
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half and then in half again, and open it out to show four boxes.
Label the boxes Morning, Daytime, Afternoon and Bedtime.
In each box, draw one ordinary thing you could ask God to help with at that time of day, like getting ready, a test, playing with friends or sleeping well.
Hold up your pictures and pray together: “Please give us what we need today.”

weeks.summary: After reading about a man who built an orphan home by trusting God, George began to pray about starting one himself and found the words “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” He asked God for a house, a large sum of money and kind helpers; the first gift was a single shilling, then came a wardrobe, a helper, and a couple who would care for the children for no pay, until the home opened with seventeen children. Speak of the orphans simply as children who needed a home and people to care for them. The big idea: God is big enough for anything, so we can bring him our biggest hopes.

memory_verse.text: I am the LORD, your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

activity.title: Little by Little
steps: Sit in a circle. The first child says, “God sent George a shilling.”
The next child repeats it and adds the next gift: “God sent George a shilling and a wardrobe.”
Keep going round, each child repeating the list and adding one more thing, such as a helper, a kind couple, a house, or anything good you can think of.
When the list gets too long to remember, everyone shouts together, “Little by little, God filled every need!”

weeks.summary: A poor young woman who sewed clothes for a few pennies a week was given a large sum of money; she paid her debts, gave a share to her mother, and brought one hundred pounds to George for the orphans. When George checked she really meant it, she said, “The Lord Jesus gave his last drop of blood for me. Should I not give him this?” and went quietly back to her plain clothes and her sewing. The big idea: you don’t have to be rich to give; a heart that loves Jesus gives cheerfully and quietly.

memory_verse.text: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart; not grudgingly, or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.

activity.title: A Secret Giver’s Card
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
Draw something cheerful on the front, like a sun, flowers or a rainbow.
Inside, write a kind message such as “Someone is thankful for you,” but do not sign your name.
Think of someone to give it to this week, at home, at school or at church, and leave it for them secretly.

weeks.summary: As more children came to the homes, there were mornings when the food nearly ran out; once the cook had only two small coins and could not buy both bread and meat, when the baker knocked and left three big loaves as a present. Looking back, George wrote that help always came before there was real hunger, and God was never late. The chapter calls God “a father to the fatherless.” Some children in your group may be fostered, adopted or without a parent, so say gently that God is a loving Father to every child, whoever looks after them, and don’t ask about anyone’s home. The big idea: God is a good Father who sees what we need and is never late.

memory_verse.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, Is God in his holy habitation.

activity.title: Held in God’s Hand
steps: Place one hand flat on a sheet of paper and trace around it with a pencil (a neighbour can help).
Write your name in the middle of the hand.
Around the outside, write “God is never late” and “God never forgets me,” and colour the hand in.
Take it home as a reminder that you are held safe by a loving Father.

weeks.summary: One morning there was hardly anything in the house, so George went to pray, and while he was still praying a message came that a lady had sent three sacks of potatoes. Another time a man in the street gave him money for the orphans; half a minute later and George would have missed him. The big idea: God sends what we need at exactly the right minute, so we can wait for him and not worry.

memory_verse.text: It shall happen that, before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

activity.title: Right on Time
activity.materials: Nothing (a watch or clock for the leader)
steps: Everyone sits down and closes their eyes.
When the leader says “Go,” count silently in your head and stand up when you think exactly 20 seconds have passed.
The leader watches the clock and tells everyone who stood up closest to the right time. Try it once more.
Talk about how hard it is to get timing just right, and how God always does: he is never too early and never too late.

weeks.summary: The orphans had porridge with milk each morning, but one evening there was no money to pay the milkman who would come before eight. At six o’clock George and two helpers knelt to ask God, and they had only just stood up when a letter arrived with a gift from someone who wrote, “I love to send these little gifts. They so often come just at the right time.” The big idea: God loves to answer prayer, even before morning comes, and those who seek him will not miss out on the good things they truly need.

memory_verse.text: The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger, but those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good thing.

activity.title: Moon and Sun Prayer Card
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half.
On one half, draw a moon and stars, and write “Tonight I trust God with…” Then draw or write one thing you will pray about at bedtime.
On the other half, draw a rising sun and write “Good morning, God. Thank you for…”
Take the card home, and look at the moon side tonight and the sun side in the morning.

weeks.summary: Visitors to the boys’ home were amazed at how well the children were cared for and assumed there must be plenty of money in the bank. The woman who ran the home, though there was hardly any money just then, answered, “Our money is kept in a bank that cannot break,” meaning God himself; the gentleman gave five pounds, which arrived just when George had not a penny left. The big idea: money can run out, but God never does, and the treasure we store with him can never be lost.

memory_verse.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal.

activity.title: Treasure That Cannot Break
steps: Draw a big treasure chest with its lid open.
Fill the chest with treasures that can never be lost, such as God’s love, kindness, prayer, friendship with Jesus and helping others.
Outside the chest, draw a few things that can break or run out, like money, toys or shoes.
Write “My treasure is safe with God” across the top, and share one treasure from your chest with a neighbour.

weeks.summary: George decided to build one great house on a hill for three hundred children, paid for only by prayer. On the thirty-sixth day of praying a thousand pounds arrived, an architect he had never met offered to plan the building for free, and the owner of a field on Ashley Down woke at three in the morning and decided to sell it to George for far less than he had planned. In time great houses stood on that hill full of hundreds of children, every brick built by prayer. The big idea: God can do more than we dream, so keep praying and wait for him patiently.

memory_verse.text: Let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

activity.title: Built by Prayer
activity.materials: A large sheet of paper and crayons
steps: Draw a big hill across a large sheet of paper and the outline of a great house on top.
Each child draws one brick on the house and writes or draws inside it something we can keep praying about, such as a friend, our church or someone who is ill.
Keep adding bricks until the house is full.
Stand around the picture and pray together for the things in the bricks, asking God to help you keep praying and keep waiting.
